questions.text: TCP client P successfully establishes a connection to TCP server [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Let [latex]N_P [/latex] denote the sequence number in the SYN sent from [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] to [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Let [latex]N_Q [/latex] denote the acknowledgement number in the SYN ACK from Q to P. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- The initial sequence number (ISN) is chosen randomly (to avoid confusion with old segments and for security) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE; it is not always 0.
- A SYN segment consumes one sequence number, so Q acknowledges with the next expected number: [latex]N_Q=N_P+1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (so [latex]N_Q=N_P[/latex] is false).

Answer: [latex]N_P[/latex] is chosen randomly by P; [latex]N_Q=N_P+1[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The sequence number [latex]N_P [/latex] is chosen randomly by [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex]
The sequence number [latex]N_P [/latex] is always 0 for a new connection
The acknowledgement number [latex]N_Q [/latex] is equal to [latex]N_P [/latex]
The acknowledgement number [latex]N_Q [/latex] is equal to [latex]N_P+1 [/latex]

questions.text:
A user starts browsing a webpage hosted at a remote server. The browser opens a single TCP connection to fetch the entire webpage from the server. The webpage consists of a top-level index page with multiple embedded image objects. Assume that all caches (e.g., DNS cache, browser cache) are all initially empty. The following packets leave the user's computer in some order.

(i) HTTP GET request for the index page
(ii) DNS request to resolve the web server's name to its IP address
(iii) HTTP GET request for an image object
(iv) TCP SYN to open a connection to the web server

Which one of the following is the CORRECT chronological order (earliest in time to latest) of the packets leaving the computer ?
questions.solution:
Order in which the packets leave the computer:
1. (ii) DNS request [latex]\text{---}[/latex] the IP address of the server is needed before anything else (caches are empty).
2. (iv) TCP SYN [latex]\text{---}[/latex] open the TCP connection with the server.
3. (i) GET index page [latex]\text{---}[/latex] first request on the connection.
4. (iii) GET image [latex]\text{---}[/latex] the browser knows about the image only after it receives and parses the index page.

Answer: (ii), (iv), (i), (iii)

questions.text:
The forwarding table of a router is shown below.
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \\ Subnet \; Number&Subnet \;Mask&Interface ID \\ \hline 200.150.0.0 &255.255.0.0& 1\\ \hline 200.150.64.0 &255.255.224.0 &2\\ \hline 200.150.68.0 &255.255.255.0 &3\\ \hline 200.150.68.64 &255.255.255.224 &4 \\ \hline Default & &0\\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
A packet addressed to a destination address 200.150.68.118 arrives at the router. It will be forwarded to the interface with ID _____.
questions.solution:
Check each entry for 200.150.68.118 (longest prefix wins):
- 200.150.0.0/16 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] matches
- 200.150.64.0/19 (third octet 64-95) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 68 matches
- 200.150.68.0/24 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] matches
- 200.150.68.64/27 (last octet 64-95) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 118 does not match

Longest match is /24 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] interface 3.

Answer: 3

questions.text:
Suppose in a web browser, you click on the www.gate-2023.in URL. The browser cache is empty. The IP address for this URL is not cached in your local host, so a DNS lookup is triggered (by the local DNS server deployed on your local host) over the 3-tier DNS hierarchy in an iterative mode. No resource records are cached anywhere across all DNS servers.
Let RTT denote the round trip time between your local host and DNS servers in the DNS hierarchy. The round trip time between the local host and the web server hosting www.gate-2023.in is also equal to RTT. The HTML file associated with the URL is small enough to have negligible transmission time and negligible rendering time by your web browser, which references 10 equally small objects on the same web server.
Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT about the minimum elapsed time between clicking on the URL and your browser fully rendering it?
questions.solution:
DNS (iterative, 3 tiers: root, TLD, authoritative) = 3 RTT.

Non-persistent, 5 parallel connections: base HTML = TCP setup + request = 2 RTT. The 10 objects go in 2 batches of 5, each batch 2 RTT (new connection each) = 4 RTT.
Total = 3 + 2 + 4 = 9 RTT.

Persistent with pipelining: TCP setup 1 RTT + HTML 1 RTT + all 10 objects pipelined in 1 RTT.
Total = 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 RTT.

Answer: 9 RTTs (non-persistent, 5 parallel) and 6 RTTs (persistent with pipelining)

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: 7 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
5 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.
9 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
6 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.

questions.text:
Suppose you are asked to design a new reliable byte-stream transport protocol like TCP. This protocol, named myTCP, runs over a 100 Mbps network with Round Trip Time of 150 milliseconds and the maximum segment lifetime of 2 minutes.
Which of the following is/are valid lengths of the Sequence Number field in the myTCP header?
questions.solution:
The sequence numbers must not wrap around within one MSL. Bytes sent in 2 minutes:
[latex]\frac{100\times10^6}{8}\times120=1.5\times10^9[/latex] bytes

[latex]2^{30}\approx1.07\times10^9[/latex] (too small), [latex]2^{31}\approx2.15\times10^9[/latex] (enough). So the field needs at least 31 bits.

32, 34 and 36 bits are valid; 30 bits is not.

Answer: 32 bits, 34 bits, 36 bits
